title: Lamia: source, date and form
short: Keats took the story from Burton's Anatomy of Melancholy, which retells Philostratus; he wrote it in summer 1819 and published it in 1820.
body: Burton tells of Menippus Lycius, a young philosopher who meets a phantom woman on the road between Cenchreas and Corinth, marries her, and loses her when the sage Apollonius exposes her as 'a serpent, a lamia'; Burton names Philostratus' Life of Apollonius, book 4, as his source. Keats printed the Burton passage at the end of the poem in the 1820 volume (Lamia, Isabella, The Eve of St. Agnes, and Other Poems). On 11 July 1819 he told Reynolds he had finished 'the 1st part which consists of about 400 lines', and on 18 September he told George he was sure there was 'that sort of fire in it' that must take hold of readers. The heroic couplets, with controlled triplets and alexandrines, were modelled on Dryden's Fables (de Sélincourt). The fairy-tale opening 'Upon a time' signals at once a told story, not myth recounted straight.

title: faery broods ... King Oberon
short: The native fairies of English folklore, ruled by Oberon, are imagined driving out the classical nymphs, satyrs, dryads and fauns.
body: Keats opens with a myth of supersession: the 'faery broods' and Oberon (king of the fairies in A Midsummer Night's Dream) have displaced the pagan woodland deities, so the tale is set in an older time before that change. Ovid, Metamorphoses 1.192-95 (which Keats could read in Sandys's translation) lists the demigods, nymphs, fauns, satyrs and woodland Silvani who inhabit the countryside, and the mixing of English fairies with classical figures was common in Elizabethan writing (compare Spenser's Faerie Queene 2.10). The opening already hints at the poem's theme of one order of belief giving way to another, as later 'cold philosophy' unweaves the rainbow.

title: ever-smitten Hermes
short: Hermes, messenger of the gods and patron of thieves, is always falling in love; he slips away from Olympus on an 'amorous theft'.
body: 'Ever-smitten' means perpetually love-struck. Hermes (Mercury) was the gods' messenger, guide of souls, and god of trickery and theft: the Homeric Hymn to Hermes tells how on the day of his birth he stole Apollo's cattle. Keats makes his escape from Olympus a theft of himself ('stolen light'), evading his 'great summoner', Jove, whose errands he normally runs. The Hermes episode is Keats's own addition to Burton; it gives the poem a divine love-story that ends happily (the gods 'grew not pale') against which the mortal love of Lycius and Lamia is measured. Ovid's story of Argus (Met. 1), in which Jove sends Hermes on an errand, is a natural background to the 'great summoner'.

title: this wreathed tomb
short: Lamia's coiled serpent body is a tomb in which a woman's self is buried alive.
body: The voice is Lamia's, lamenting her imprisonment in snake form: 'wreathed' describes the coils, and 'tomb' makes the body a grave. She longs for 'a sweet body fit for life', for 'the ruddy strife / Of hearts and lips'. Keats thus introduces her as a sufferer whose cry 'destroys / All pain but pity' in a gentle heart, an echo of the medieval commonplace, familiar from Dante's circle, that love and pity repair to the gentle heart. Her first appearance invites sympathy, which complicates the later question whether she is victim or demon. Later the narrator calls the snake form her 'serpent prison-house'.

title: cirque-couchant
short: A Keatsian compound: lying coiled in a circle.
body: 'Cirque' is a circle or ring (Latin circus); 'couchant' is the heraldic term for a beast lying down with its head raised. Keats combines them, in a heraldic manner, for the snake lying in rings in a 'dusky brake' (thicket). The heraldic vocabulary prepares for the blazon-like description that follows, in which Lamia's body is catalogued colour by colour like a coat of arms or a jewelled tapestry. Readers have differed on whether coinages like this one are lapses or deliberate signs of the poem's artifice.

title: a gordian shape of dazzling hue
short: Her body is knotted like the Gordian knot, and blazoned in every colour, like zebra, leopard and peacock at once.
body: The Gordian knot, tied by King Gordius of Phrygia, was so intricate that only Alexander's sword could undo it; 'gordian' here means intricately coiled. The catalogue that follows ('Vermilion-spotted, golden, green, and blue; / Striped like a zebra, freckled like a pard') piles up exotic comparisons: a pard is a leopard, and the peacock's 'eyes' and the 'silver moons' that dissolve and brighten as she breathes make her a living, shifting jewel. The excess is deliberate: she is dazzling, unnatural and composite, a creature of art as much as nature. The richness recalls Elizabethan romance description, notably Spenser.

title: some penanced lady elf, / Some demon's mistress, or the demon's self
short: The narrator cannot decide what Lamia is: an enchanted woman doing penance, a demon's lover, or a demon. The poem never fully settles it.
body: The three-way alternative is the poem's central uncertainty. A 'penanced lady elf' is a fairy woman under a spell, suffering; a 'demon's mistress' or 'the demon's self' points to the lamia of Philostratus and Burton, a fiend who feeds on young men. Critics have long divided. Some read Lamia sympathetically, as a figure of imaginative beauty or of passion destroyed by Apollonius' 'cold philosophy'; others stress her deceit and the illusion of her palace, as in Burton, where all her furniture is 'no substance, but mere illusions'. Many recent readers argue that Keats deliberately keeps both possibilities open, so that the reader's sympathy is divided between Lamia, Lycius and Apollonius. Note too that she is 'touch'd with miseries': the line begins with pity.

title: like Ariadne's tiar
short: Ariadne's crown, set among the stars by Bacchus, is the constellation Corona Borealis.
body: Ariadne, deserted by Theseus on Naxos, was wedded by Bacchus, who set her crown in the heavens as a constellation (Ovid, Met. 8.176-82). 'Tiar' is a poetic form of tiara. Editors have compared Titian's Bacchus and Ariadne (National Gallery), where a ring of stars appears above Ariadne's head, and Spenser's Faerie Queene 6.10.13 on the crown Ariadne wore. Lamia's 'wannish fire / Sprinkled with stars' thus links her with another abandoned woman raised to glory by a god; it is also the last part of her serpent beauty to vanish ('Still shone her crown').

title: As Proserpine still weeps for her Sicilian air
short: Proserpine, carried off to the underworld from Sicily, still mourns her lost upper world, as Lamia mourns her lost woman's shape.
body: Proserpine (Persephone) was seized by Pluto while gathering flowers at Enna in Sicily (Ovid, Met. 5.385 ff.). The comparison makes Lamia's beautiful eyes, made only to weep, the eyes of a captive longing for a lost life. The line is an alexandrine closing a triplet, a Drydenian device. Milton's lines on 'that faire field / Of Enna' (Paradise Lost 4.268-72) were a well-known version of the story, and Keats knew them well. The allusion adds to the sympathetic reading of Lamia as a victim imprisoned against her will.

title: the star of Lethe
short: Hermes, who leads the souls of the dead down to Lethe and the underworld, shines like a star among them.
body: Hermes Psychopompos guided the dead to Hades (Odyssey 24.1-14, where he drives the suitors' ghosts with his golden wand). Lethe is the underworld river of forgetfulness; Hermes is its 'star' as the one bright presence in that dim region. The phrase was singled out by Charles Lamb in his review of the 1820 volume (New Times, 19 July 1820), where he admired the compression of the phrase for the god. Lamia answers him with a similar epithet, 'Bright planet' (l. 87).

title: my serpent rod ... the lythe Caducean charm
short: Hermes' caduceus, a wand twined with two serpents, is the instrument of his magic; he uses it to give Lamia a woman's form.
body: The caduceus (Greek kerykeion, herald's staff) was Hermes' golden wand, which in later iconography is twined with two snakes; Homer gives it power to charm men's eyes to sleep or wake them. Hermes fittingly swears 'by my serpent rod' to a serpent, and with 'languid arm' he 'put to proof' (tested, exercised) its 'lythe' (lithe, supple) power on her. The scene is a bargain: Lamia reveals the invisible nymph, and the god transforms Lamia.

title: her Circean head
short: Like Circe, the enchantress of the Odyssey, Lamia is a dangerous sorceress who can transform.
body: Circe turned Odysseus' men into swine (Odyssey 10). The epithet tilts the ambiguity towards the demonic: Lamia is at once a pleading victim and an enchantress with power of her own (she has made the nymph invisible with 'weird syrops'). Ravish'd by Hermes' oath, she lifts her Circean head and 'Blush'd a live damask', the colour of the damask rose, the first colour of a woman's life in the poem.

sources.cite: Homer, Odyssey 10.133-574

anchor: Real are the dreams of Gods
title: It was no dream; or say a dream it was, / Real are the dreams of Gods
short: For gods, dream and reality are the same; for mortals, as the poem will show, they are not.
body: The narrator first denies, then concedes, that Hermes' vision was a dream, and resolves the doubt by saying that the dreams of gods are real. The lines recall Keats's letter to Bailey of 22 November 1817: 'The Imagination may be compared to Adam's dream,--he awoke and found it truth' (alluding to Paradise Lost 8.478-84). In Lamia the gods enjoy that unity of dream and truth, and their love does not fade ('Nor grew they pale, as mortal lovers do'). The mortal Lycius lives in a dream too, but his will be broken by Apollonius' gaze. Critics read the contrast as Keats testing his own earlier faith in the imagination.

title: Nor grew they pale, as mortal lovers do
short: The happy end of the gods' affair sets up its opposite: mortal love fades and grows pale.
body: The line closes the Hermes episode with a pointed comparison. The nymph's fearful fading 'like a moon in wane' is reversed by the god's warmth, and she blooms 'like new flowers' (the 'self-folding' flower that 'faints into itself at evening hour' recalls Paradise Lost 9.278, 'at shut of Evening Flours'). The contrast between immortal and mortal passion is a recurring Keatsian concern, as in the Ode on a Grecian Urn, where painted lovers stay 'For ever warm' while 'breathing human passion' leaves 'a heart high-sorrowful and cloy'd'. Lycius at the end of Part II will literally grow pale and die.

title: The transformation: 'A deep volcanian yellow'
short: Lamia's change to woman is violent and painful, described as a volcanic eruption that burns away her jewelled serpent skin.
body: The metamorphosis is not a gentle Ovidian change but a convulsion: she foams, her eyes flash 'phosphor', 'volcanian yellow' spreads over her like lava 'ravishing' a meadow, and her 'silver mail, and golden brede' (scaly armour and embroidery) are spoilt. 'Brede' means embroidery or interwoven work; Keats uses it again in the Ode on a Grecian Urn ('brede / Of marble men and maidens'), and in both places he probably meant 'embroidery', remembering Collins's Ode to Evening ('brede ethereal wove'). The cost of becoming human is pain; the passage reverses the earlier catalogue of her beauty item by item ('Eclips'd her crescents, and lick'd up her stars').

title: Cenchreas ... Peræan rills ... Cleone
short: Lamia waits on the road from Corinth's eastern port to the city, the very road of Burton's story.
body: Cenchreae (Keats's 'Cenchreas', after Burton) was one of Corinth's two harbours, on the Saronic Gulf; the other was Lechaeum on the Corinthian Gulf (Strabo 8.6.22). Lycius is returning by sea from a sacrifice at Jove's temple on Aegina ('Egina isle'), across the gulf. The 'Peræan rills' probably refers to the Peraea, the promontory opposite Corinth across the gulf (modern Perachora), and Cleone is Cleonae, a town south-west of Corinth on the road to Argos. The precise place-names give the fairy-tale a surface of geographical fact, as Burton's account also has.

sources.cite: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy (1621), Part. 3, Sect. 2, Memb. 1, Subs. 1

title: in Cupid's college ... kept his rosy terms
short: Lamia, though 'not one hour old' and a virgin, is learned in love as if she had graduated from a university of Cupid.
body: The passage is a witty paradox: 'A virgin purest lipp'd, yet in the lore / Of love deep learned'. Her 'sciential brain' (knowing, from Latin scientia) can 'unperplex bliss from its neighbour pain', separating pleasure from the pain that borders it, as though dissecting atoms. The academic conceit follows: she has 'kept his rosy terms' (university terms, with a pun on terms of art) as 'a lovely graduate, still unshent' (unharmed, unreproached; from 'shend', to disgrace). The Drydenian, half-satirical tone here has troubled some readers, who find the narrator's worldly irony at odds with the poem's romance; others see it as Keats's deliberate distance from his material.

title: Pluto's gardens palatine / Mulciber's columns
short: In her dreams Lamia visits the underworld, where the columns built by Mulciber (Vulcan) stand in long colonnades.
body: Lamia's spirit roams the mythical world: Elysium, Thetis' sea-palace, Bacchus' revels under a 'glutinous' (resinous) pine, and Pluto's 'palatine' (palatial) gardens. Mulciber is the Roman fire-god Vulcan, the divine smith; the name echoes Paradise Lost 1.740, where Mulciber is the architect of Pandemonium. 'Piazzian' (like a piazza's colonnade) is another coinage. The Miltonic echo quietly associates Lamia's dream-palaces with the infernal architecture of Pandemonium, anticipating the illusory palace she will raise in Corinth.

sources.cite: Milton, Paradise Lost 1.730-51

title: the calm'd twilight of Platonic shades
short: Lycius is a philosopher, lost in abstract thought; his reason fades into Platonic reverie just as Lamia appears.
body: Burton calls the young man 'a philosopher, otherwise staid and discreet, able to moderate his passions, though not this of love'. Keats renders this as a mind 'lost, where reason fades, / In the calm'd twilight of Platonic shades': 'shades' are both the groves of the Academy where Plato taught and the shadowy forms of idealist thought. Lamia later calls him 'a scholar'. The phrasing prepares for the poem's conflict between philosophy and passion: Lycius' mind is 'wrapp'd like his mantle', closed to the world, and so open to enchantment.

title: Orpheus-like at an Eurydice
short: Lycius looks back at Lamia as Orpheus looked back at Eurydice, an ominous comparison, since Orpheus' backward look lost her forever.
body: Lamia calls 'Lycius, look back!', and he does. In Ovid (Met. 10.1-63), Orpheus, leading Eurydice up from the underworld, turns to look at her too soon and she slips back among the dead. Keats's simile says Lycius looks with longing, not 'cold wonder', but the myth carries a warning: this love, too, is begun by a forbidden glance and will end in loss. The 'syllabling' voice just before recalls Comus 208, 'airy tongues that syllable men's names', an unearthly, dangerous summons.

sources.cite: Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.1-63

title: a descended Pleiad
short: Lycius imagines Lamia might be one of the seven Pleiades come down from the sky, leaving her sisters to keep her star in tune.
body: The Pleiades were the seven daughters of Atlas, set in the heavens as a star cluster; since only six are easily visible, the myth of a 'lost Pleiad' (often Merope, who married a mortal) was widespread. Lycius' flattering guesses run through Naiad (river nymph), wood-nymph and Pleiad. The lines invoke the music of the spheres: one of 'thine harmonious sisters' would have to 'keep in tune / Thy spheres' and shine as her 'silver proxy'. Lamia's reply (ll. 280-85) turns the compliment into a reason to refuse: finer spirits cannot breathe in human climes. The note of a goddess who descends to mortal love is again ominous.

title: lineal indeed / From Pyrrha's pebbles or old Adam's seed
short: No fairy or goddess is as delightful as a real woman, descended either from the stones of Greek myth or from biblical Adam.
body: After the flood, Deucalion and Pyrrha repeopled the earth by throwing stones over their shoulders, which became men and women (Ovid, Met. 1.313-415). Pairing them with Adam is the habit of Sandys's commentary on Ovid, which matches classical and biblical stories; compare Paradise Lost 11.8-14, where Adam and Eve are likened to 'Deucalion and chaste Pyrrha'. 'Peris' are the beautiful spirits of Persian legend, made fashionable by Thomas Moore's Lalla Rookh (1817). The irony is sharp: the narrator praises 'a real woman' just as Lamia, who is no such thing, plays 'woman's part'.

title: The Adonian feast
short: The Adonia, a festival of mourning for Adonis, Venus' young lover killed by a boar, held with baskets of quick-growing herbs.
body: Lamia claims she first saw Lycius at Venus' temple 'mid baskets heap'd / Of amorous herbs and flowers', on the eve of the Adonia. At this festival women lamented Adonis and set out 'gardens of Adonis', shallow pots of quickly sprouting, quickly withering plants, a proverb for brief life. The allusion is apt and sinister: Adonis is the beautiful youth loved by a goddess and early destroyed, as Lycius will be. The story of Venus and Adonis is told in Ovid (Met. 10.503-739) and in Spenser's Garden of Adonis (Faerie Queene 3.6).

title: Apollonius sage
short: Apollonius of Tyana, the first-century sage whose life Philostratus wrote; in the poem he is Lycius' teacher and Lamia's nemesis.
body: Apollonius of Tyana was a Neopythagorean philosopher and wonder-worker; Philostratus' Life of Apollonius (4.25) tells how he exposed the 'empusa' or 'lamia' who had ensnared his pupil Menippus. Keats's first sketch of him ('curl'd gray beard, sharp eyes, and smooth bald crown') already makes him a figure of penetrating sight; Lamia trembles and cannot 'bring to mind / His features', and Lycius calls him 'the ghost of folly haunting my sweet dreams'. In Part II his 'cold philosophy' will 'unweave a rainbow'. Readers divide over whether he is the poem's villain or its truth-teller; Keats seems to give each side its due.

title: Sounds Æolian / Breath'd from the hinges
short: The doors of Lamia's palace sigh like an Aeolian harp, a sign of enchantment.
body: The Aeolian harp, named after Aeolus, god of the winds, was a stringed box played by the wind, a favourite Romantic image (Coleridge's 'The Eolian Harp', 1795). Here music breathes from mere hinges, and the palace's marble is so 'unsullied' that 'none but feet divine / Could e'er have touch'd there': it is too perfect to be real. Like the 'few Persian mutes' who serve it and whose dwelling no one can trace, everything about the house points to illusion, the 'Tantalus's gold' of Burton's story, which will vanish when Apollonius sees through it.
